title: The role and scope of the autonomous midwife
blurb: Explain the midwife's role as accountable lead professional, its legal limits, and what happens when care needs an obstetrician.
question: In a midwifery-led unit, a woman in established labour has a single blood pressure reading of 162/104 mmHg. Her midwife has cared for her since booking. What is the midwife's role now?

teach.body: SPM 1.6 asks the midwife to be accountable and autonomous as the lead professional for the midwifery care of women and newborn infants across the whole continuum: pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, labour and birth, postpartum and the early weeks of life. Autonomous means she makes and owns her own clinical decisions; accountable means she can explain and justify them. In plain English: for a woman with a straightforward pregnancy, the midwife can lead care from start to finish without a doctor.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives (2019) 1.6, 1.7

teach.caption: SPM 2.11: the midwife coordinates care and arranges seamless transfer (to health visitor and GP) when midwifery care is complete.

teach.h: The legal basis of the role
teach.body: Article 45 of the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001 makes it an offence for anyone other than a registered midwife or registered medical practitioner to attend a woman in childbirth, except in sudden or urgent necessity or as a student on a recognised course. Midwives can also administer certain medicines without a prescription under the midwives exemptions in Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012.
teach.cite: Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001 art 45; Human Medicines Regulations 2012 Sch 17

teach.caption: Student midwives may give Part 3 medicines under direct supervision, but not diamorphine, morphine or pethidine.

teach.h: When does care need an obstetrician?
teach.caption: Complications do not end the midwife's role: she provides ongoing midwifery care, coordination and advocacy.

teach.h: Examples of NG235 transfer triggers in labour
head: Finding
Threshold
rows: Over 120 on 2 occasions 15 to 30 min apart
Diastolic 90+ or systolic 140+, 2 readings 15 to 30 min apart
teach.caption: NICE NG235 1.8.20 and 1.8.50. An epidural is available only in obstetric units.

teach.h: Scenario: Hannah in the midwifery-led unit
teach.body: Hannah is in established labour in an alongside midwifery unit. Her BP is 162/104 mmHg on a single reading: systolic 160 or more meets an NG235 transfer trigger. Her midwife, Ruth, explains the finding and the reason for transfer, escalates to the obstetric team and arranges transfer to the obstetric unit. Ruth keeps caring for Hannah there as her midwife, coordinating care and making sure Hannah's birth preferences travel with her.

teach.text: Shared or obstetric-led care is not 'handing the woman over'. The obstetrician leads on the complication; the midwife remains accountable for her midwifery care and advocacy. Equally, autonomy is not working alone: Code 13.2 and 13.3 require timely referral and asking for help beyond your competence.

items: SPM 1.6: accountable, autonomous lead professional for midwifery care across the whole continuum.
NMO 2001 art 45: only a midwife or doctor attends a woman in childbirth, except urgent necessity or students.
HMR 2012 Sch 17 midwives exemptions cover medicines such as oxytocin, pethidine and naloxone; not tranexamic acid or magnesium sulfate.
Deviation from normal: recognise, respond, refer and escalate; the midwife keeps caring as part of the MDT.

summary: You can now explain the midwife's role as accountable, autonomous lead professional and its legal basis. You can recognise when care must involve an obstetrician and describe the midwife's continuing role once it does.

A.q: Under the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001, who may attend a woman in childbirth, outside sudden or urgent necessity?
options: A registered midwife or registered doctor
Any registered nurse or paramedic
A trained maternity support worker
A doula with recognised training
A.why: Article 45 restricts attending a woman in childbirth to registered midwives and registered medical practitioners, except in sudden or urgent necessity or recognised students.

whyNot.1: Nurses and paramedics are not included in article 45, outside urgent necessity.
whyNot.2: Support workers can assist a midwife but may not attend a woman in childbirth themselves.
whyNot.3: A doula gives emotional support but may not attend a woman in childbirth as a clinician.

A.q: During a home birth, a midwife needs to give a uterotonic for active management of the third stage. Which of these can she give under the midwives exemptions without a prescription?
options: Misoprostol
Tranexamic acid
Magnesium sulfate
Oxytocin
A.why: Oxytocins (natural and synthetic) are listed in Schedule 17 Part 3 for administration by registered midwives.

whyNot.0: Misoprostol is not on the midwives exemptions list and needs a prescription or PGD.
whyNot.1: Tranexamic acid is not on the midwives exemptions list.
whyNot.2: Magnesium sulfate is not on the midwives exemptions list.

A.q: Which statement best describes the midwife's role when a woman develops a complication in pregnancy?
options: The obstetrician takes over all of her care
The midwife refers and continues midwifery care
The midwife discharges her to the GP
The midwife continues care without referral
A.why: The SPM role statement: the midwife recognises, responds and escalates, and keeps responsibility for continuity and coordination, providing ongoing midwifery care within the MDT.

whyNot.0: Obstetricians lead on the complication, but midwifery care does not stop.
whyNot.2: Discharge to the GP would leave her without maternity care.
whyNot.3: A complication needs referral (Code 13.2); continuing alone is outside the midwife's scope.

B.q: A woman in a freestanding midwifery unit has a maternal pulse of 124 bpm, rechecked 20 minutes later at 126 bpm. What should the midwife do?
options: Recheck the pulse in one hour
Offer oral fluids and observe
Arrange transfer to obstetric-led care
Start intermittent auscultation every 5 minutes
B.why: NG235 1.8.20: a maternal pulse over 120 on 2 occasions 15 to 30 minutes apart is a trigger for transfer to obstetric-led care.

whyNot.0: The trigger has already been met; waiting another hour delays transfer.
whyNot.1: Fluids may help, but the finding meets the transfer criterion.
whyNot.3: Changing the auscultation interval does not address the maternal finding.

B.q: A student midwife is supervised by her practice supervisor at a birth. Which medicine may she NOT administer under the midwives exemptions?
options: Oxytocin
Pethidine
Vitamin K
Anti-D immunoglobulin
B.why: Student midwives may administer Schedule 17 Part 3 medicines under direct supervision, but not diamorphine, morphine or pethidine.

whyNot.0: Oxytocin can be given by a student midwife under direct supervision.
whyNot.2: Phytomenadione (vitamin K) can be given by a student midwife under direct supervision.
whyNot.3: Anti-D immunoglobulin can be given by a student midwife under direct supervision.

B.q: A woman with a low-risk pregnancy asks whether she has to see a doctor during her pregnancy. Which answer is most accurate?
options: A doctor must see her at booking
A doctor must confirm her birth plan
A midwife can lead all her care
A GP must review her at 36 weeks
B.why: SPM 1.6: the midwife is the accountable lead professional for women across the continuum; with a straightforward pregnancy, care can be midwife-led throughout.

whyNot.0: Booking is a midwife appointment; there is no requirement for a doctor.
whyNot.1: Birth plans are made with her midwife; no doctor's sign-off is needed.
whyNot.3: There is no routine GP review required at 36 weeks for low-risk women.

C.q: A woman in established labour at a birth centre wants an epidural. She is otherwise low risk. What should the midwife explain?
options: Epidural is available after an anaesthetic phone review
Epidural needs transfer to an obstetric unit
Epidural can be sited by an experienced midwife
Epidural is not advised in a first labour
C.why: NG235: regional analgesia is available only in obstetric units, so the woman would need to transfer. The midwife explains this, along with alternatives, so she can choose.

whyNot.0: A phone review does not make an epidural possible in a birth centre.
whyNot.2: Epidurals are sited by anaesthetists, not midwives.
whyNot.3: First labour is not a reason to advise against an epidural.

C.q: A woman under midwife-led care is transferred to the obstetric unit with delay in the first stage. Her midwife is asked to stay with her. What best describes the midwife's responsibility there?
options: Observe while the obstetric team manages care
Hand over and return to the birth centre
Lead decisions about oxytocin and birth
Provide midwifery care within the MDT
C.why: The midwife provides ongoing midwifery care and continuity as part of the multidisciplinary team, coordinating and advocating; the obstetrician leads on the complication.

whyNot.0: She is not a passive observer; she is still giving midwifery care.
whyNot.1: She has been asked to stay; continuity of carer benefits the woman.
whyNot.2: Decisions about augmentation and mode of birth after confirmed delay need obstetric review.

C.q: A community midwife is called to a woman labouring quickly at home. On arrival, the woman's mother, a retired nurse, has already delivered the baby. Under article 45, how is the mother's action best described?
options: An offence, as she is not a midwife
Lawful, as sudden or urgent necessity
Lawful, because she was a registered nurse
An offence unless she called 999 first
C.why: Article 45 allows attendance in childbirth by someone other than a midwife or doctor in sudden or urgent necessity, as in a rapid unplanned birth.

whyNot.2: Being a nurse does not by itself permit attending childbirth; the exception is urgent necessity.
whyNot.3: Calling 999 is sensible, but it is not a condition of the exception.

reteach.title: Lead, refer, stay
reteach.question: What three words sum up the midwife's role when pregnancy moves away from normal?

blocks.body: LEAD: for straightforward pregnancies, the midwife is the lead professional from pre-pregnancy to the early weeks after birth. REFER: when something deviates from normal, she recognises it, responds at once and escalates to the right colleague. STAY: she continues to give midwifery care, coordinate and advocate for the woman, now as part of a wider team.

steps.label: Stay
steps.sub: Ongoing midwifery care in the MDT

blocks.text: Remember article 45: a registered midwife or registered doctor attends a woman in childbirth. Others may help only in sudden or urgent necessity, or as recognised students.

explain.body: SPM 1.6: accountable and autonomous lead professional for midwifery care across the whole continuum. She makes, explains and justifies her own decisions.

test.q: What does 'autonomous' mean in the description of the midwife as lead professional?
options: She works without other professionals
She can prescribe any maternity medicine
She makes and owns her clinical decisions
She sets her own clinical guidelines
test.why: Autonomy means the midwife makes and owns her own clinical decisions, and is accountable for them.

whyNot.0: Autonomous practice still involves referral and teamwork.
whyNot.1: Midwives administer listed medicines under exemptions; prescribing needs a prescribing qualification.
whyNot.3: Midwives follow evidence-based guidance; autonomy does not mean writing their own.

explain.body: Article 45 restricts attending childbirth to midwives and doctors (except urgent necessity and students). Schedule 17 lets midwives give listed medicines without a prescription.

test.q: Which medicine is listed for administration by registered midwives under Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012?
options: Naloxone hydrochloride
Tranexamic acid
Low molecular weight heparin
Benzylpenicillin
test.why: Naloxone hydrochloride is on the Schedule 17 Part 3 list, used for neonatal respiratory depression after maternal opioids.

whyNot.1: Tranexamic acid is not on the list.
whyNot.2: LMWH is not on the list.
whyNot.3: Antibiotics are not on the list.

explain.body: Midwives anticipate and recognise changes that may lead to complications and are responsible for immediate response, management and escalation. NG235 gives transfer triggers in labour.

test.q: A woman labouring at home has a single blood pressure of 128/112 mmHg. What does NG235 advise?
options: Repeat the reading in 30 minutes
Recheck after she has emptied her bladder
Transfer to obstetric-led care
Repeat the reading in 15 minutes
test.why: A single diastolic of 110 or more is a trigger for transfer to obstetric-led care (NG235 1.8.20).

whyNot.0: Two readings 15 to 30 minutes apart apply to diastolic 90 or more or systolic 140 or more; a single diastolic of 110+ triggers transfer.
whyNot.1: A full bladder does not explain this reading, and delay is unsafe.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a repeat delays transfer that is already indicated.

explain.body: When complications arise the midwife keeps 'specific responsibility for continuity and coordination of care', giving ongoing midwifery care in the MDT and advocating for the woman.

test.q: A woman with pre-eclampsia is now under obstetric-led care on the labour ward. Which task remains the midwife's responsibility?
options: Coordinating her ongoing care
Choosing the antihypertensive
Deciding the timing of birth
Ordering the mode of birth
test.why: The midwife keeps responsibility for continuity and coordination of care and gives ongoing midwifery care within the MDT.

whyNot.1: Choosing antihypertensive medicine is a medical prescribing decision.
whyNot.2: Timing of birth in pre-eclampsia is an obstetric decision with the woman.
whyNot.3: Mode of birth for a complicated pregnancy is decided with the obstetric team and the woman.
